blockingFinding.what: A kept copy whose drain claimed it (advanced the role's cursor past it) but never forwarded it is lost: no later drain offers it, and its sender was answered 202 kept. This breaks the tree's rule that a 202 kept message is never lost and the worst case is a duplicate the holder drops by its key. It is the cost the implementer's own handoff states for finding 2's fix ('a drain that dies between its claim and its forward loses that one copy'), raised to a blocking finding by INFRA-514's architect on 2026-10-31.
blockingFinding.evidence: Red test TestAKeptCopyItsDrainNeverForwardedStillReachesTheRolesHolder, pushed to legion/INFRA-839-wip at f84cd3600e66 (packages/envoy/cmd/listener/role_keep_loss_test.go). It keeps one copy for an unheld role, runs a drain whose forwardRole returns an error (the deterministic stand-in for a death between the claim and the forward, which is a cursor write and a core-NATS forward apart — a few ms — and which no timed kill reproduced live, see proof[kill]), then runs a replacement drain for the same holder and asserts the copy still reaches it. At code head 2d7167658086 it fails: `role_keep_loss_test.go:65: the kept copy under envoy.role.forward.kept-claimed-then-lost-00 reached no holder after the drain that claimed it ended before forwarding it; the replacement drain handed over []`. The defect is wider than a crash: claimKeptRoleCopy (role_keep.go:305) advances the cursor before forwardKeptRoleMessage (role_keep.go:345), and any forward failure other than bus.ErrReceiptTimeout returns from drainKeptRole with the cursor already past the copy, so a transient bus/receipt error loses the copy with no crash at all.
blockingFinding.remedy: The architect settled claim, forward, confirm: the cursor body gains a field {kept, claiming}; a drain compare-and-swaps to {kept:k, claiming:s} before forwarding copy s, forwards, then compare-and-swaps to {kept:s, claiming:0}; a drain that reads claiming>kept re-forwards that copy under its stable id before going on, so a death yields a duplicate the holder drops rather than a loss. Not forward-first, which would reintroduce finding 2 (two drains, two holders).

proof.observed: All six copies reached exactly one holder (A or B), none reached both, none reached neither: 'exactly once: 6, never: 0, more than once: 0'.

proof.criterion: A keep landing while a claim is being written reaches that holder (review finding 5).
proof.surface: One real listener; ten role topics, each with a publish and a claim fired concurrently, and twelve more with the publish started first and the claim ~4ms later.
proof.command: bash $TMPDIR/tester/multi.sh (section C); bash $TMPDIR/tester/probe.sh listener-new head (section F)
proof.observed: Every one of the 22 raced messages reached the session that claimed the role, exactly once. In these live races the publish's first holder resolution won and answered 200 (delivered live) rather than 202; the branch where the keep wins the race and drainAfterKeep delivers is pinned deterministically by TestAKeptCopyReachesTheHolderThatClaimedTheRoleUnderTheKeep (pinVerification finding 5), which fails in 20s without drainAfterKeep.
proof.negativeControl: Reverting drainAfterKeep makes the unit test wait out 20s and fail; the live races that landed as 200 are the control that the holder is reached whichever path wins.

proof.criterion: kill: a listener killed mid-drain. Does every kept copy still reach a holder?
proof.surface: Two real listeners; twelve copies kept for an unheld role, A claims and begins its drain, A is SIGKILLed after its first forward line, B then claims and drains.
proof.observed: All twelve reached a holder; the timed kill did not land in the loss window. The window is a cursor write and a core-NATS forward apart (a few ms), so a timed kill does not reproduce it reliably — which is why the loss is pinned by the deterministic red test on legion/INFRA-839-wip (blockingFinding) rather than by this kill, exactly as the architect and implementer anticipated.
proof.negativeControl: The red test fails the copy's forward at the same point a crash would strike and shows the copy lost; this live kill is the complement that shows a timed kill alone is not a reliable probe.
